title: Optimal competitive ratio for convex body chasing
formal:
Determine, up to universal constant factors as a function of \(d\), the optimal deterministic competitive ratio \(\mathcal C(d)\) for general convex body chasing in Euclidean space \(\mathbb R^d\). The domain is every integer \(d\ge1\).

An online strategy starts at \(x_0=0\), sees a nonempty compact convex set \(K_t\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) at round \(t\), and must immediately choose \(x_t\in K_t\) using only \(K_1,\ldots,K_t\). Its cost on a finite request sequence is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|x_t-x_{t-1}\|_2\). Let
\[\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)=\min_{y_t\in K_t,\ y_0=0}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\|y_t-y_{t-1}\|_2\]
and define
\[\mathcal C(d)=\inf\left\{c\ge1:\ \exists A\ \forall T\ge1\ \forall K_1,\ldots,K_T,\quad\operatorname{cost}_A(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\le c\,\operatorname{OPT}(K_1,\ldots,K_T)\right\}.\]
The strategy may depend on \(d\), but must serve all horizons and request sequences in that dimension. The target is the asymptotic order of this dimension-dependent ratio, resolving the source's gap between order \(\sqrt d\) and order \(d\).
why: Convex body chasing isolates the movement cost of maintaining feasibility when constraints arrive without advance notice. The optimal dependence on dimension measures how much geometric complexity alone can penalize online decisions, independently of computational efficiency. Matching bounds would resolve a central quantitative gap between what convexity permits offline and what an online strategy can guarantee.

progress.text: Friedman and Linial introduce convex body chasing; the later sources describe its finite-competitiveness conjecture and the square-root Euclidean obstruction.

The SODA results give linear dimension dependence for general requests, and a nearly square-root Euclidean bound for the nested variant. Sellke’s revised full manuscript separately states the horizon-dependent Euclidean improvement.
Gupta’s Winter School slides continue to distinguish the linear general bound, the nearly square-root nested bound, and the square-root Euclidean lower bound.

importance.reason: A canonical geometric model of online optimization with movement costs.

category_assignment.reason: The main target is the cost or competitive ratio of serving requests without knowledge of the future.

sentences: Convex body chasing requires an online player to move into each newly revealed convex set.
The player pays Euclidean movement while an offline comparator knows all future requests.
This question asks for the optimal deterministic competitive ratio as dimension grows, up to universal constant factors.
The strategy must work for arbitrary finite request sequences without knowing the horizon.
The checked sources leave a gap between square-root and linear dimension dependence for general requests, with stronger results only in restricted settings.

definitions:
The Euclidean norm is \(\|v\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}v_j^2)^{1/2}\). A request set is nonempty, compact and convex: it is closed and bounded, and contains \((1-\lambda)u+\lambda v\) whenever \(u,v\) lie in it and \(0\le\lambda\le1\). Lower-dimensional sets, including points and faces of polytopes, are allowed. There is no common diameter bound, containment relation or promise that consecutive requests intersect. In particular, the sequence need not be nested.

A deterministic online strategy is a sequence of maps \(A_t\), one for every positive integer \(t\), taking every length-\(t\) request history to a point in its final set. These maps jointly specify one causal strategy: two request sequences with the same prefix have the same choices on that prefix, irrespective of their eventual lengths or later requests. Its own previous locations are determined by that history. The full current set is available before choosing the current point; no future set, horizon, forecast, advice or random choice is supplied.

This is the information-theoretic model of competitive analysis used in the sources. Strategies are mathematical maps on convex sets, with unrestricted computation; a finite input encoding, polynomial-time evaluator or bounded number of membership queries is not an extra requirement. An answer must specify its strategy well enough to prove feasibility and cost, but the benchmark measures movement, not computational time.

The offline comparator starts at the same origin, knows the whole finite sequence, and may choose a different feasible point at every round. Compactness makes its displayed minimum attainable. There is no required return to the origin and no additional service cost or cost for reading a request. Competitiveness is a purely multiplicative guarantee on every finite sequence, with no additive constant. If OPT is zero, the online strategy must also incur zero cost; the definition uses an inequality to avoid division by zero. Requests may be selected adversarially after previous moves, since the guarantee covers every finite request history for a deterministic strategy.

The infimum is over all qualifying ratios and strategies in each dimension; it need not be attained. Its value is finite by the known dimension-dependent upper bound. Determination up to universal factors means providing a noncircular positive function \(h\) on the positive integers and constants \(a,b>0\), independent of dimension, such that \(a h(d)\le\mathcal C(d)\le b h(d)\) for every \(d\ge1\). Equivalent eventually valid asymptotic bounds may be extended over the finitely many smaller dimensions by adjusting constants. The question does not require an exact ratio or an additive \(1/100\) estimate of that ratio.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked determination of the asymptotic growth of \(\mathcal C(d)\), with matching upper and lower bounds up to universal constant factors. The upper bound must cover arbitrary finite, possibly non-nested request sequences with one horizon-independent deterministic strategy in each dimension. The lower bound must apply to every permitted strategy. A nonattained infimum may be handled by arbitrarily approaching bounds. Merely renaming the optimization defining \(\mathcal C\), proving a bound for nested requests, allowing the ratio to grow with the horizon, or establishing a lower bound in another norm does not meet the criterion.

context_blocks.text: The 2025 source lists an \(O(d)\) upper bound for general convex body chasing and an \(\Omega(\sqrt d)\) lower bound in Euclidean space. It separately lists the stronger upper bound for nested requests; the saved card concerns the unrestricted sequence problem.

Sellke proves a competitive ratio of \(d\) for convex body chasing in an arbitrary \(d\)-dimensional normed space. That dependence is tight for the maximum-coordinate norm, but the corresponding general Euclidean lower bound is only of order \(\sqrt d\). A worst-case norm cannot be substituted for the fixed Euclidean norm here.

For Euclidean requests of horizon \(T\), Sellke also proves an \(O(\sqrt{d\log T})\) guarantee. Combining it with the dimension-only bound helps at shorter horizons, but it does not yield a sublinear-in-d bound uniformly over arbitrary \(T\).

The nested problem adds \(K_{t+1}\subseteq K_t\). Its \(O(\sqrt{d\log d})\) Euclidean upper bound is nearly the square-root lower bound, but that extra containment hypothesis is not available in this card. Recent applications to shrinking feasible regions therefore do not by themselves close the general chasing gap.
